feature_results.rationale: Cursor documents a native hooks mechanism configured via .cursor/hooks.json (repo-scoped) or ~/.cursor/hooks.json (user-scoped) that runs user-supplied shell commands at defined points across the agent's action lifecycle: beforeShellExecution, afterShellExecution, beforeReadFile, afterFileEdit, preToolUse, postToolUse, postToolUseFailure, subagentStart, subagentStop, and preCompact. A hook receives a JSON payload on stdin and can print a JSON permission decision (allow/deny/ask) on stdout, or use exit code 2 to block the action, satisfying the requirement that hooks can influence/block (not just passively observe) the agent's action. Coverage spans pre/post tool-call and shell-execution events generally, not a single narrow lifecycle point, so this exceeds the partial_criteria ceiling.

evidence.excerpt: {"permission": "allow"}" or "{"permission": "deny", "user_message": "Destructive command blocked"}
Exit code 2 from command hooks blocks the action (equivalent to returning permission: "deny").
hooks running before or after defined stages of the agent loop and able to observe, block, or modify behavior

constraints.description: Hooks are configured in .cursor/hooks.json inside a repository (checked into version control) or in ~/.cursor/hooks.json in a user's home directory; they are opt-in scripts an admin/user must author rather than a built-in policy.

cursor.com/docs/hooks.md permission decision block deny approve tool call
cursor.com blog hooks-partners hooks security platform teams observe block modify

feature_results.rationale: Cursor's cloud/background agent sandbox lets a customer define exactly which domains the agent may reach via a sandbox.json allow-list, with three configurable levels of network access (restrict to your allow-list, allow-list plus Cursor defaults, or unrestricted). Enterprise admins can additionally enforce organization-wide network allow-lists/deny-lists from the admin dashboard, applying egress policy to all agent sandbox sessions.

evidence.excerpt: you can now define exactly which domains the agent is allowed to reach while running sandboxed commands. The sandbox supports three levels of network access: restrict to domains in your sandbox.json, restrict to your allowlist plus Cursor's built-in defaults, or allow all network access within the sandbox.
Admins on the Enterprise plan can enforce network allowlists and denylists from the admin dashboard, ensuring organization-wide egress policies apply to all agent sandbox sessions.

constraints.description: Organization-wide enforcement of egress allow-lists/deny-lists from the admin dashboard is an Enterprise-plan admin control; per-session sandbox.json scoping applies to cloud/background agent sessions.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor's Checkpoints feature (in Agent chat) lets a user restore the full agent session's file state to any earlier point in the conversation in one operation, undoing every file change the Agent made since that point, not just a single file or hunk. This is a documented, session-wide restore mechanism distinct from per-hunk diff accept/reject, satisfying the has_criteria for session-wide checkpoint/rollback.

evidence.excerpt: Restoring a checkpoint will reset all files to that point in the conversation.

constraints.description: Checkpoints cover only Agent-made changes within the current session/recent history and are automatically cleaned up over time; Cursor's own docs state checkpoints are not a substitute for Git version control.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor's Bugbot is a dedicated, documented automated PR-review workflow: it reviews pull requests automatically when a PR is opened or updated, reads the full diff context (including how changed code interacts with the rest of the codebase), and surfaces bugs, security issues, and code-quality problems as review comments. A separate Autofix capability can spawn cloud agents that propose fixes for issues it finds. This goes well beyond ad hoc chat-based code review, satisfying the has_criteria.

evidence.excerpt: Bugbot reviews pull requests and identifies bugs, security issues, and code quality problems.
Bugbot can now find and automatically fix issues in PRs, spawning cloud agents that work independently in their own virtual machines to test your software.

constraints.description: Bugbot operates on pull requests through a connected repository/VCS (e.g. GitHub) integration; it is not a chat-only review capability.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor documents a file-based custom-subagent authoring mechanism: Markdown files with YAML frontmatter placed under .cursor/agents/, each defining the subagent's own name/description (persona and effective system prompt), a tools field that scopes which tools the subagent may call (or a readonly flag restricting it to read-only actions), and frontmatter that can also configure disallowed tools, MCP servers, hooks, max turns, skills, and background behavior. This is a documented, supported extension mechanism for authoring a new role with its own prompt and independently scoped tool access, going beyond the fixed built-in agent roles, and matches the has_criteria.

evidence.excerpt: Subagents are specialized AI assistants that Cursor's agent can delegate tasks to. Each subagent operates in its own context window, handles specific types of work, and returns its result to the parent agent.
The readonly field can be set to true to restrict write permissions. When set to true, the agent should only read and analyze, never write files, which is useful for auditors and reviewers.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor's official SDK changelog documents a native, non-MCP registration surface: developers pass function definitions through local.customTools on Agent.create() (or per send()) in the Cursor Agent SDK, and Cursor explicitly contrasts this with the prior requirement of standing up a full stdio/HTTP MCP server. This is a documented API/config surface for registering a callable function/tool that does not require the developer to build or wire in an external MCP server, matching has_criteria; it is scoped to the Cursor SDK (for building custom agent-powered applications) rather than a setting inside the standard IDE chat/agent UI.

evidence.excerpt: You can now hand the local agent your own tools by passing function definitions through local.customTools, on Agent.create() or per send().
Before this, exposing a custom capability meant standing up your own stdio or remote HTTP MCP server and wiring it into the agent. Now a function definition is enough.

constraints.description: Documented for the Cursor Agent SDK (TypeScript/Python, for building custom programmatic agent applications), not as a setting exposed within the standard Cursor IDE chat/agent UI.

Internally, the SDK exposes registered custom tools to the model through a built-in MCP server ('custom-user-tools'), so calls are routed through the same permission gate as other MCP tools even though the developer-facing registration surface is a plain function definition rather than standing up an MCP server.

feature_results.rationale: No official Cursor source states that the whole product (core AI functionality plus surrounding product operation) functions with zero network connectivity. Cursor's own documentation and enterprise/pricing pages describe network-dependent architecture: an official Network Configuration doc covers proxy configuration, IP allowlisting, and required outbound connectivity (not an offline mode); Cursor's changelog documents 'self-hosted' Cloud Agents that keep code and tool execution on infrastructure the customer controls, but this is a deployment-location option for the agent runtime, not a fully-disconnected/air-gapped operating mode, and it still depends on network connectivity between components. The pricing page (cursor.com/pricing) and the enterprise page describe plan tiers, SSO, audit logs, and cloud-based security/compliance controls, with no mention of offline or air-gapped operation. No changelog entry, docs page, product page, or pricing page claims zero-network operation. All relevant source classes (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing) were checked via targeted searches with no unresolved access gaps; the searches consistently surfaced only network-dependent architecture and user requests for offline/air-gapped support that Cursor has not (per these official pages) fulfilled.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor's Master Services Agreement (the negotiated contract used for organizations with a signed Order Form, i.e. Enterprise-tier customers) contains a stated IP indemnification commitment: Anysphere indemnifies the Customer against third-party claims that the Service or a Suggestion infringes or misappropriates third-party IP rights, subject to standard carve-outs (customer disabled safety/content filters, customer knew or should have known the Suggestion was likely infringing, or customer lacked lawful rights over the Customer Data used to generate the Suggestion). This appears tied to organizations with a negotiated MSA rather than to the standard individual Free/Pro Terms of Service, under which the indemnification flows the other way (customer indemnifies Anysphere). Checks of cursor.com's documentation (cursor.com/docs), product/security pages (cursor.com, cursor.com/security), pricing (cursor.com/pricing), changelog (cursor.com/changelog), and blog (cursor.com/blog) found no description of a configurable filter that blocks code suggestions matching public code, comparable to GitHub Copilot's 'duplication detection filter'. Community forum threads on forum.cursor.com show users repeatedly asking whether Cursor offers such a filter, with no confirmation from Cursor of such a feature. Per the feature's partial_criteria, only one of the two qualifying mechanisms (the IP indemnification commitment) is documented, and that mechanism itself is restricted to a specific commercial arrangement (negotiated Enterprise MSA), so status is partial rather than has or not_found.

evidence.excerpt: Anysphere shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Customer, its Affiliates, and each of their officers, directors, employees, and agents from and against any and all claims, lawsuits, losses, damages, liabilities, and costs (including reasonable attorneys' fees) arising out of any third-party claim that the Service or any Suggestion infringes or misappropriates such third party's intellectual property rights.

constraints.description: The indemnification commitment is set out in Cursor's Master Services Agreement (MSA), which governs organizations that have a negotiated agreement/Order Form with Anysphere (i.e. Enterprise-tier customers), rather than individual Free/Pro users under the standard Terms of Service.

Anysphere's indemnification obligation for a Suggestion does not apply if the Customer disabled or interfered with content filters/safety systems, knew or should have known the Suggestion was likely to infringe a third party's rights, or lacked lawful rights over the Customer Data used to generate the Suggestion.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor's official documentation confirms a documented mechanism for pointing the tool at a customer-controlled model endpoint rather than only Cursor's own cloud-hosted models: Settings > Models exposes an 'Override OpenAI Base URL' option for a custom model, and Cursor's own enterprise documentation states that a custom model reached via an OpenAI-compatible base URL override (or a third-party gateway) carries the region of that gateway/model - confirming this custom-model path is an officially documented, supported mechanism rather than an unsupported workaround. Because self-hosted local inference backends such as Ollama expose an OpenAI-compatible API, this documented base URL override is the supported way community guides use to run Cursor against a self-hosted/local model. However, this falls short of full 'has' status: Cursor's own documentation and independent reporting consistently indicate the custom-model endpoint must be reachable over the network (a public URL or gateway), because Cursor's backend participates in the request path rather than the client connecting directly to a purely local/offline endpoint - so a strictly air-gapped, localhost-only model is not directly supported without exposing it. Cursor also does not market or document this generically as 'local model support' (e.g. no dedicated Ollama/local-model documentation page was found); the local-model use is a documented-mechanism-plus-community-application rather than a first-class, explicitly named local/offline model feature. This combination of a real but narrower/constrained supported path meets partial_criteria rather than has_criteria or not_found.

evidence.excerpt: Custom models reached via an OpenAI-compatible base URL override or a third-party gateway carry the region of that gateway or model, which may not be in the US.
you can point Cursor's custom OpenAI base URL at LLM Gateway to use any of our 200+ models in the AI panel — both plan mode and agent mode

constraints.description: The custom-model base URL override requires a network-reachable endpoint (a public URL or gateway); Cursor's backend remains part of the request path, so a purely offline/localhost-only model is not directly supported without exposing it via a gateway or tunnel.

A custom model reached via base URL override or a third-party gateway carries the region of that gateway/model; if the organization has US-only data residency enabled, a non-US-region custom/local model becomes unavailable.

feature_results.rationale: Cursor documents a repository-scale context mechanism beyond raw model context-window size: files are split into syntactic chunks and converted into cached embeddings so unchanged chunks are reused rather than re-processed, and Cursor further reuses near-identical existing indexes across a team's highly similar codebase copies to keep large-repository indexing fast and current, satisfying the has_criteria.

evidence.excerpt: When a file changes, Cursor splits it into syntactic chunks, which are converted into embeddings that enable semantic search. Cursor caches embeddings by chunk content, so unchanged chunks hit the cache, allowing agent responses to stay fast.

Cursor found ways to speed up indexing based on the observation that most teams work from near-identical copies of the same codebase (averaging 92% similarity across users within an organization), allowing secure reuse of existing indexes rather than rebuilding from scratch.

use_cases.title: Onboarding developers to large, unfamiliar codebases
use_cases.description: A new team member (or a developer picking up a large legacy repository) can rely on semantic, natural-language search over the whole indexed codebase plus persistent, per-project memory of prior conversations to build understanding of unfamiliar code and conventions faster than manual exploration alone, without re-explaining project context in every session.
use_cases.rationale: codebase_semantic_search documents natural-language retrieval across the indexed project; long_context_large_repo_handling documents that this indexing scales efficiently to large repositories; persistent_project_memory documents that facts from conversations and versioned project conventions are automatically retained and reapplied across sessions. Together these capabilities plausibly support faster onboarding, though no single official source frames this as a named 'onboarding' use case.

use_cases.title: Running many independent coding tasks in parallel across a team
use_cases.description: A team runs numerous independent coding tasks concurrently - each developer's own agents in isolated Git worktrees locally, plus additional cloud/background agents running unattended - so throughput on a backlog of small, independent tasks scales with the number of agents rather than being serialized through one session at a time.
use_cases.rationale: parallel_independent_task_execution documents the Agents Window/worktrees mechanism for running multiple independent agent sessions concurrently; multi_agent_orchestration documents subagent delegation and parallel cloud/background agent execution; background_long_running_tasks documents cloud agents continuing unattended without blocking a user's local session. Combined, these support a team-scale parallel-throughput workflow, though this exact framing is not a named official use case.

use_cases.title: Scheduled and event-triggered agent automations
use_cases.description: Teams configure a cloud agent to run on a cron schedule or in response to an event - a GitHub/GitLab pull request, a Slack message, a Linear issue, or a generic webhook - so recurring or reactive engineering work (e.g. dependency bumps, triage, report generation) happens without an active user session initiating it.

evidence.excerpt: An automation is a cloud agent that runs on a schedule or in response to an event, including a schedule (cron) or an event like a GitHub/GitLab PR, a Slack message, a Linear issue, or a generic webhook.
Cursor's agents run on schedules or are triggered by events like a sent Slack message, a newly created Linear issue, a merged GitHub PR, or a PagerDuty incident.

use_cases.title: Generating and backfilling unit test coverage
use_cases.description: Cursor maintains a dedicated official workflow for using the Agent to write unit tests targeting specified functions or files, backfill missing test coverage on an existing codebase, and build broader test automation.

evidence.excerpt: How to use Cursor to write unit tests, backfill coverage, and build test automation.

release_history.summary: Published at cursor.com/changelog/06-18-26. Adds an /automate skill to create an automation directly from a local agent session by describing the task in plain language, Slack emoji-reaction triggers, five new GitHub triggers (issue comment, PR review comment, PR review submitted, review-thread updated, workflow run completed), computer-use support so automation-started cloud agents can produce demos/screenshots/artifacts, and usability improvements (saving automations through MCP auth, opening PRs by default, cleaning up outdated memory files).

evidence.excerpt: Improvements to Cursor Automations · Cursor

release_history.version: Canvas Design Mode and Context Usage Report
release_history.summary: Published at cursor.com/changelog/canvas-improvements. Adds a Design Mode to Cursor's canvases allowing direct selection and annotation of UI elements to instruct edits, plus a Context Usage report showing interactive token-allocation detail; also documents shared canvases opening full-screen in the browser, agent-embeddable buttons that run a specific prompt when clicked, improved canvas type-error fixes, and expanded chart customization.

evidence.excerpt: Canvas Design Mode and Context Usage Report · Cursor

release_history.summary: Published at cursor.com/changelog/enterprise-organizations. Makes 'Organizations' generally available to all Enterprise customers: an organization is documented as the top-level container for a company's identity, administration, and membership, letting admins manage multiple Cursor teams from one place with different security, governance, budget, and feature controls per team, plus a rollup view of spend and token usage across every team.

evidence.excerpt: Organizations for Cursor Enterprise · Cursor

release_history.summary: Cursor's official iOS app entered public beta, giving direct access to the assistant from a phone: launching and controlling coding/cloud agents, voice input, model selection, and reviewing or merging pull requests, rather than only account or billing management.

evidence.excerpt: Cursor Mobile App for iOS · Cursor

release_history.summary: Published at cursor.com/changelog/3-0. Introduced a redesigned Cursor interface built around running many agents in parallel across repositories and environments, ahead of the subsequent 3.x releases (worktree-based parallel agents, canvases, organizations, and automations improvements) captured elsewhere in this release history.

evidence.excerpt: New Cursor Interface

release_history.version: Custom stores, custom tools, and auto-review for the Cursor SDK
release_history.summary: Adds local.customTools to the Cursor Agent SDK (TypeScript and Python), letting a developer hand the local agent its own callable tools via function definitions on Agent.create() or per send() instead of standing up a stdio/HTTP MCP server; adds auto-review routing for local tool calls via a permissions.json-steered classifier, configurable persistence of agent/run metadata (including JSONL and custom stores) with nested subagents to any depth, and a set of reliability/performance/platform fixes for running local and cloud SDK agents in production scripts, CI, and custom integrations.

evidence.excerpt: You can now hand the local agent your own tools by passing function definitions through local.customTools, on Agent.create() or per send().

release_history.summary: Published at cursor.com/changelog/side-chat. Introduces side chats - durable secondary agent conversations that branch off a running chat via /side, /btw, or the plus button, carry context from the main chat, and can be @-mentioned to pull results back into the main thread - plus agent transcript search (a local search index over past conversations, searchable from the Agents Window command palette and within a conversation via Cmd+F), simplified project/repo pickers, and five new cloud-agent hook events for observing conversations, prompts, responses, thinking, subagents, and turn completion.

evidence.excerpt: Side Chats and Conversation Search · Cursor

release_history.version: MCPs and Organizations in Team Marketplaces
release_history.summary: Published at cursor.com/changelog/team-marketplace-updates. Lets admins configure Team MCP servers once and distribute them to cloud agents, the Agents Window, the IDE, and the CLI via a governed Team Marketplace (Dashboard -> Integrations & MCP); team marketplaces now also support organization-group-based access control alongside existing SCIM directory-group support, so admins can restrict marketplace access to specific organization groups (Dashboard -> Plugins -> Team Marketplaces).

evidence.excerpt: MCPs and Organizations in Team Marketplaces · Cursor

unresolved_issues.description: Five of the eight release_history entries (side-chat, team-marketplace-updates, 06-18-26 automations, canvas-improvements, enterprise-organizations) are hosted at specific dated cursor.com/changelog/* URLs that were not individually present in this task's known_sources registry; only the general changelog root (cursor_changelog) was available, so evidence for those entries cites cursor_changelog with the specific post's title as excerpt, and the specific URL is named in each entry's `summary` for traceability. A future source-discovery pass should register these five URLs as first-party changelog sources.

Several recent cursor.com/changelog posts captured in release_history are commonly labeled by third-party trackers/aggregators with sequential version numbers (e.g. '3.6' through '3.11'), but the official page URLs/titles for those specific posts (side-chat, team-marketplace-updates, 06-18-26, canvas-improvements, enterprise-organizations) do not themselves expose a matching numeric version, and WebFetch is unavailable in this environment to directly confirm one from the rendered page. Per the release_history version-labelling rule, this worker used each post's official title as `version` rather than an unconfirmed third-party version number, and only assigned `product_version` (3.0) to the one entry (New Cursor Interface) whose URL slug itself contains a version number consistent with other known changelog sources (e.g. /changelog/2-4, /changelog/1-3).

As with the already-merged feature_results in this run, WebFetch is unavailable in this environment. The pricing figures cited in the 'pricing_tiers' additional fact and the SOC 2/GDPR/CCPA compliance wording cited in 'data_usage_compliance' are reconstructed from WebSearch's summarized rendering of cursor.com/pricing and cursor.com/security rather than a direct page fetch, though the numeric figures were independently corroborated across multiple unrelated third-party pricing trackers, which were used only to locate and corroborate the official page's content, not as the basis for the facts themselves.
